title: The Pyramids of Egypt
summary: Why the ancient Egyptians built the pyramids of Giza, how paid workers moved and raised millions of heavy stone blocks, and why the Great Pyramid still amazes the world.
poll: People long ago were just as clever as people today.

versions.title: The Big Stone Tombs
versions.text:
See the huge stone shapes in the sand? They are pyramids. They stand in Egypt. The Nile is near. They were built long, long ago.

Each one was a tomb. A tomb is a place to bury the dead. These were for kings. A king of Egypt was a pharaoh.

The Great Pyramid is the biggest. It was built for a king. His name was Khufu. It has more than two million stone blocks. Some weigh more than a car! It took about 20 years to build.

How did they move the big stones? Boats took them on the Nile. Then men put them on a sledge. A sledge is a big sled. They poured water on the sand. Then it could slide. They pulled the blocks up a ramp. A ramp is a slope.

The men were paid. They lived in a town close by.

Each side faces a way: north, south, east, or west. For a long time, no one built a thing as tall. You can still see it! Folks come from far to see it.

The men who did this were paid. They lived in a town close by.

The sides of the Great Pyramid face north, south, east, and west. For thousands of years, it was the tallest thing that people had built. You can still see it now!

versions.title: The Pyramids of Egypt
versions.text:
Huge stone shapes rise from the sand in Egypt. They are the pyramids. They stand near the Nile River. People built them about 4,500 years ago.

Each pyramid was a tomb. A tomb is a place where the dead are buried. These tombs were built for kings. In Egypt, a king was called a pharaoh.

The biggest one is the Great Pyramid. It was built for a pharaoh named Khufu. It is made of more than two million stone blocks. Many blocks weigh more than a car! It took about 20 years to build.

How did people move such big stones? First, boats carried many of them on the Nile. Then workers put each block on a sledge. A sledge is a big wooden sled. They poured water on the sand in front of it. This made the sledge slide more easily. Then they dragged the blocks up a ramp, which is a long slope.

The workers were not slaves. They were paid, and they lived in a town nearby.

Each side of the Great Pyramid faces north, south, east, or west. For thousands of years, it was the tallest thing people had ever built. It still stands today.

versions.title: The Pyramids of Egypt
versions.text:
Huge stone shapes rise from the desert sand in Egypt. These are the pyramids of Giza, which stand near the Nile River, close to the city of Cairo. People built them about 4,500 years ago.

Each pyramid was a tomb. A tomb is a place where people are buried. These giant tombs were built for the kings of ancient Egypt, who were called pharaohs. Kings were buried with treasures, but robbers took most of them long ago.

The biggest pyramid is the Great Pyramid. It was built for a pharaoh named Khufu. It contains more than two million stone blocks, and many of them weigh more than a car. It took about 20 years to build it.

How did people move such heavy stones? Boats carried many of them along the Nile. Then workers put each block on a sledge, which is a big wooden sled. They poured water on the sand in front of it so the sledge would slide more easily. To lift the blocks higher, they dragged them up a ramp, a long slope made of dirt and stone.

The builders were not slaves. They were paid workers who lived in a nearby town with homes and bakeries.

Each side of the Great Pyramid faces north, south, east, or west. For thousands of years, it was the tallest building in the world. It still stands today.

versions.title: The Pyramids: Wonders of Stone
versions.text:
Huge stone shapes rise from the desert sand in Egypt. These are the pyramids of Giza, which stand near the Nile River, close to the city of Cairo. People built them about 4,500 years ago, long before trucks or cranes existed.

Each pyramid was a tomb, a place where someone was buried. These giant tombs were built for the kings of ancient Egypt, who were called pharaohs. Pharaohs were buried with gold and other treasures, but robbers took most of these riches long ago.

The largest is the Great Pyramid, which was built for a pharaoh named Khufu. It was originally about 146 meters tall and contains more than two million stone blocks. Many of the blocks weigh more than a car. Building it took about 20 years.

Most of the blocks are limestone. Workers cut them from a quarry right next to the pyramid. Smooth white limestone for the outside came from across the river, and hard granite was carried by boat from Aswan, far to the south.

To move the heavy stones, workers placed each block on a wooden sledge. They poured water on the sand in front of it, because wet sand made the sledge slide more easily. To raise the blocks higher, they dragged them up ramps. The builders were not slaves. They were paid workers who lived in a nearby town, and skilled engineers planned their work.

Each side of the Great Pyramid faces almost exactly north, south, east, or west. For about 3,800 years, it was the tallest building in the world. It is also the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still stands today.

versions.title: The Pyramids: Wonders of Stone
versions.text:
Enormous stone shapes rise from the desert sand in Egypt. These are the pyramids of Giza, which stand near the Nile River, close to the modern city of Cairo. They were constructed approximately 4,500 years ago by one of the world's earliest great civilizations, long before trucks, cranes, or iron tools existed.

Each pyramid served as a tomb for one of the kings of ancient Egypt, who were known as pharaohs. The pyramid shape developed gradually. An earlier pharaoh, Djoser, was buried in a step pyramid, which resembles a stack of gigantic stone platforms, and later builders learned to create smooth, straight sides.

The largest monument at Giza is the Great Pyramid, which was built for a pharaoh named Khufu. It originally stood about 146 meters tall and contains more than two million stone blocks, many of which weigh more than an automobile. Its construction required about 20 years.

Most of the blocks are limestone extracted from a quarry beside the pyramid. Polished white limestone for the outer layer was transported from across the river, while heavy granite was delivered by boat from Aswan, far to the south. Archaeologists have even discovered an ancient diary, written by an official named Merer, that describes boats carrying limestone to Giza.

To move the stones, workers positioned each block on a wooden sledge and poured water on the sand in front of it, because damp sand reduced friction and allowed the sledge to slide more easily. They then hauled the blocks up ramps. The builders were not slaves but paid laborers who lived in a nearby town equipped with bakeries and homes, and skilled engineers carefully organized their work.

Each side of the Great Pyramid faces almost exactly north, south, east, or west, which demonstrates how precise its builders were. For about 3,800 years, it remained the tallest structure in the world, and it is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still survives.

versions.title: The Pyramids: Building a Mountain of Stone
versions.text:
Enormous stone monuments rise from the desert plateau of Giza, near the Nile River and the modern Egyptian capital, Cairo. They were constructed approximately 4,500 years ago by one of humanity's earliest sophisticated civilizations, centuries before iron tools, cranes, or modern machinery existed. They continue to fascinate historians, engineers, and travelers alike.

Each pyramid functioned as a monumental tomb for one of the rulers of ancient Egypt, who were known as pharaohs. The distinctive shape evolved gradually. An earlier pharaoh, Djoser, was buried in a step pyramid, which resembles a stack of gigantic stone platforms. Later architects experimented until they could build smooth, sloping sides.

The most celebrated monument at Giza is the Great Pyramid, which was commissioned for the pharaoh Khufu. It originally stood approximately 146 meters tall and incorporates more than two million stone blocks, many of which weigh more than an automobile. Its construction took roughly twenty years of carefully coordinated effort.

Most of the blocks are limestone extracted from a quarry immediately adjacent to the pyramid. Polished white limestone for the exterior casing was transported from quarries across the river. Massive granite beams were delivered by boat from Aswan, hundreds of kilometers to the south. Archaeologists have even recovered an extraordinary ancient diary, composed by an official named Merer, which documents vessels transporting limestone to Giza along specially excavated canals.

To relocate the stones on land, laborers positioned each block on a wooden sledge and poured water onto the sand ahead of it, because moistened sand dramatically reduced friction and allowed the heavy sledge to glide considerably more easily. The workers subsequently hauled the blocks up inclined ramps, although historians continue to debate precisely how these ramps were designed and arranged. Contrary to a popular belief, the builders were not slaves but compensated laborers who resided in a nearby settlement equipped with bakeries, dwellings, and even their own cemeteries.

Each side of the Great Pyramid is aligned almost exactly with north, south, east, or west, which demonstrates how remarkably precise its designers were despite their simple tools. For approximately 3,800 years it remained the tallest human-made structure on Earth, and today it is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still survives, a lasting testament to the ingenuity and organization of Egyptian civilization.

versions.title: The Pyramids: Building a Mountain of Stone
versions.text:
Enormous geometric stone monuments rise dramatically and imposingly from the arid desert plateau of Giza, situated near the Nile River and the modern Egyptian capital, Cairo. These remarkable architectural structures were constructed approximately 4,500 years ago by one of humanity's earliest sophisticated and highly organized civilizations, centuries before the subsequent development of iron tools, mechanical cranes, or any form of modern industrial machinery whatsoever. They continue to fascinate professional historians, structural engineers, and casual travelers alike across successive generations of human curiosity.

Each individual pyramid functioned specifically and exclusively as a monumental tomb constructed for one particular ruler of ancient Egyptian civilization, rulers who were formally and ceremonially designated pharaohs. The distinctive pyramidal architectural shape evolved gradually across successive generations of royal builders and architects. An earlier pharaoh, Djoser, was ceremonially interred within a step pyramid, an architectural structure resembling a series of progressively smaller stacked stone platforms arranged in diminishing tiers, while subsequent generations of architects experimented extensively and iteratively until they successfully achieved smooth, uniformly sloping pyramid sides.

The single most celebrated monument situated at the Giza plateau is unquestionably the Great Pyramid, which was specifically commissioned for construction by the pharaoh Khufu. It originally stood approximately 146 meters in total height and incorporates more than two million individual stone blocks, many of which individually weigh considerably more than a modern automobile. Its complete architectural construction required roughly twenty years of carefully coordinated, continuously sustained organizational labor involving thousands of workers.

The overwhelming majority of the constituent structural blocks consist of ordinary limestone extracted directly from a quarry situated immediately adjacent to the pyramid construction site itself. Polished white limestone specifically intended for the exterior decorative casing was transported laboriously from separate quarries located across the Nile River, while massive granite structural support beams were delivered by boat from distant Aswan, hundreds of kilometers to the south along the river. Archaeologists have even successfully recovered an extraordinary ancient papyrus diary, composed meticulously by an Egyptian official named Merer, which documents in considerable detail vessels transporting limestone to Giza along specially excavated artificial canal waterways constructed for this precise logistical purpose.

To relocate these enormous stone blocks across considerable overland distances, laborers would carefully position each individual block upon a wooden sledge and deliberately pour water onto the sand directly ahead of it, since moistened sand dramatically and measurably reduced frictional resistance, allowing the heavily laden sledge to glide considerably more easily across the arid terrain. Workers subsequently hauled these massive blocks upward along inclined construction ramps, although historians and archaeologists continue vigorously debating precisely how these elaborate ramps were originally designed and structurally arranged during construction. Contrary to a persistent, widespread popular misconception, the builders were demonstrably and verifiably not enslaved laborers but rather compensated, salaried workers who resided within a nearby purpose-built settlement equipped with functioning bakeries, residential dwellings, and even their own dedicated burial cemeteries.

Each individual side of the Great Pyramid is aligned almost exactly and precisely with true cardinal north, south, east, or west, a remarkable architectural and surveying achievement that demonstrates with considerable clarity how extraordinarily precise its ancient designers and surveyors truly were despite possessing only comparatively simple, rudimentary measuring instruments. For approximately 3,800 consecutive years, it remained unambiguously the tallest human-constructed structure anywhere on Earth, and today it remains the sole surviving architectural structure among the original Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, constituting a genuinely lasting testament to the remarkable ingenuity and organizational sophistication of ancient Egyptian civilization across the millennia.

questions.why: Since the blocks were so heavy, cutting them nearby meant less dragging over long distances.

wrong.A: The article does not say this.
wrong.B: The article gives no such reason.
wrong.C: The article says boats carried granite and white limestone, so they did use boats.

questions.stem: The builders were paid workers who lived in a nearby town. What does this suggest?
options: The work was organized and skilled.
The workers only came for one day.
Nobody wanted to work on the pyramids.
The town was built after the pyramid.
questions.why: Paying workers and housing them nearby shows that the project was carefully organized, as the article says engineers planned the work.

wrong.B: The work took about 20 years, so workers stayed much longer.
wrong.C: The article does not suggest this.
wrong.D: The workers lived in the town while building, so it existed during the work.

questions.stem: "It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still stands." What does wonder mean here?
options: A question that has no answer
A small statue made of gold
Something amazing that people admire
A tomb that has been robbed
questions.why: The Seven Wonders were amazing things that people admired; the Great Pyramid is the last one standing.

wrong.A: Wonder can mean to ask yourself something, but here it names an amazing structure.
wrong.B: The Great Pyramid is not a small gold statue.
wrong.D: Being robbed is not what makes something a wonder.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe where each kind of stone came from?
options: To show how far and how carefully materials were moved
To persuade readers to visit Aswan
To explain why limestone is white
To list all the cities in Egypt
questions.why: Describing the nearby quarry, the river crossing, and the boats from Aswan shows the effort and planning behind the work.

wrong.B: The article does not try to persuade readers to travel.
wrong.C: The article does not explain the color of limestone.
wrong.D: Only a few places are named, not all cities.

questions.stem: What happened after workers placed a block on a sledge and wet the sand?
options: They carved treasures into the block.
They sent the block back to the quarry.
They loaded it onto a boat to Aswan.
They dragged it, then raised it up ramps.
questions.why: The article explains that the sledge slid over the wet sand, and then the blocks were dragged up ramps to raise them higher.

wrong.A: The article does not describe carving treasures.
wrong.B: Blocks came from the quarry; they were not sent back.
wrong.C: Granite came from Aswan; blocks were not sent there.

MID.prompt: Explain how the ancient Egyptians moved such heavy stones without modern machines. Use at least three details from the article in the right order.
checklist: I explained the steps in order.
I used at least three details from the article.
I used order words such as first, next, and finally.
MID.modelAnswer: First, workers cut huge blocks of limestone from a quarry right beside the pyramid. Next, they placed each block on a wooden sledge and poured water on the sand in front of it, because wet sand let the sledge slide more easily. Finally, they dragged the blocks up ramps to raise them higher, while skilled engineers carefully organized the whole process. This ancient system let people build a wonder of the world without any modern machines.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The pyramids prove that Egypt had more workers than any other land.
The Great Pyramid shows an early civilization's skill.
Djoser's step pyramid is more important than the Great Pyramid.
The pyramids were built mainly to attract visitors.

wrong.A: The article never compares the number of workers with other lands.
wrong.C: Djoser's pyramid is an earlier step in the shape's development, not the focus.
wrong.D: The pyramids were built as tombs, not to attract visitors.

questions.stem: What does Merer's diary describe?
options: Boats carrying limestone to Giza
How Djoser's step pyramid was designed
The treasures buried with Khufu
Daily life in the town of Cairo
questions.why: The article says Merer's diary describes boats carrying limestone to Giza.

wrong.B: The article does not connect Merer to Djoser.
wrong.C: The diary is about transport, not treasure.
wrong.D: Cairo is a modern city, and the diary is not about it.

questions.stem: How did the shape of pyramids change over time?
options: They grew taller but kept stepped sides.
They began smooth and later became stepped.
They changed from round to square.
They went from stepped sides to smooth sides.

wrong.A: Later pyramids have smooth sides, not steps.
wrong.B: This reverses the order in the article.
wrong.C: The article never describes round pyramids.

questions.stem: Why is it important that the builders lived in a nearby settlement with bakeries and homes?
options: It shows the pyramids were built in a single year.
It proves the pharaohs lived in the town.
It supports the idea that they were paid laborers.
It shows the workers did not need food.
questions.why: A town where workers lived and were fed supports the article's point that they were paid laborers rather than slaves.

wrong.B: The town was for workers, not pharaohs.
wrong.D: Bakeries show the workers were fed, which is the opposite.

questions.stem: The sides of the Great Pyramid face almost exactly north, south, east, and west. What can you infer about its builders?
options: They built it in a hurry.
They measured directions carefully.
They used modern compasses and machines.
They did not care about the pyramid's shape.
questions.why: Such exact alignment, as the article calls it precise, means the builders measured carefully even without modern tools.

wrong.A: Precise work suggests care, not haste.
wrong.C: The article says the pyramids were built long before modern machinery.
wrong.D: Their careful alignment shows they cared a great deal.

questions.stem: The article says the builders were remarkably precise. What does precise mean?
options: Exact and careful
Quick and noisy
Rich and powerful
Strong and tall

wrong.B: Speed and noise have nothing to do with alignment.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention Djoser's step pyramid?

wrong.C: The article does not say step pyramids are taller.
wrong.D: Merer is not connected to Djoser in the article.

questions.stem: According to the article, why did wet sand help the workers?
options: It made the blocks lighter.
It hardened into a stone road.
It cooled the workers' tired feet.
It let the sledge slide more easily.
questions.why: The article states that damp sand allowed the sledge to slide more easily.

HIGH.prompt: The article suggests the pyramids are a testament to human skill and organization. Do you agree? Support your answer with at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that the pyramids are a testament to human skill and organization, because building the Great Pyramid required an extraordinary level of planning. First, paid laborers organized by skilled engineers moved more than two million stone blocks, some weighing more than a car, using only wooden sledges and wetted sand. Second, builders transported smooth limestone from across the river and heavy granite by boat all the way from Aswan, showing a precise system for sourcing different materials. Third, each side of the Great Pyramid faces almost exactly north, south, east, or west, an accuracy that still impresses archaeologists today. Such a massive, carefully coordinated monument could only have come from a highly organized civilization.
